cards.prompt: Compute a 3-day rolling average of ts's revenue. Fill in the blank.
cards.why: rolling(3) creates a moving window of 3 consecutive rows; .mean() then aggregates each window — the first 2 rows have no full window yet, so they're NaN.
cards.whenToUse: Smoothing noisy time-series data to see the underlying trend.
cards.commonMistake: Expecting a value for every row — by default the first window_size - 1 rows are NaN, since there isn't a full window yet.

cards.prompt: Compute a 3-day rolling total of ts's revenue instead of the average. Fill in the blank.
cards.why: Any aggregation (.sum(), .max(), .std()...) can follow rolling() — the window mechanics stay the same, only the aggregation changes.
cards.whenToUse: A trailing total over a fixed number of periods, e.g. '3-day rolling sales.'
cards.commonMistake: Confusing a rolling sum with cumsum() — rolling only includes the last n rows, cumsum includes everything from the start.

cards.prompt: Compute a 3-day rolling average, but allow a result even for the first couple of rows that don't have a full window yet. Fill in the blank.
cards.why: min_periods lowers how many observations are required before producing a value — with min_periods=1, row 0 averages over just itself.
cards.whenToUse: You'd rather see a partial-window estimate at the start of the series than a run of NaNs.
cards.commonMistake: Setting min_periods higher than the window size — that's a no-op at best and raises for some window types, since you can never have more observations than the window itself.

cards.prompt: Compute a running average of ts's revenue using every row seen so far, not just a fixed-size window. Fill in the blank.
cards.why: expanding() grows the window by one row at a time from the start of the series, unlike rolling()'s fixed-size window.
cards.whenToUse: A 'running average to date' metric, like year-to-date performance.
cards.commonMistake: Reaching for rolling() with a huge window size to fake this — expanding() says the intent directly and needs no window-size guess.

cards.prompt: Get yesterday's revenue value alongside every row (shift the Series forward by 1). Fill in the blank.
cards.why: shift(1) moves every value down one position, so row n shows what was at row n-1 — the classic way to compare 'this period vs. last period.'
cards.whenToUse: Computing period-over-period comparisons, or building a lag feature.
cards.commonMistake: Assuming shift() reorders or drops rows — it keeps every row's position, just fills the newly-empty first slot with NaN.

cards.prompt: Compute the day-over-day change in ts's revenue. Fill in the blank.
cards.why: diff() is shorthand for value - value.shift(1) — the absolute change from the previous row.
cards.whenToUse: Highlighting day-to-day swings rather than the raw level.
cards.commonMistake: Confusing diff() (absolute change) with pct_change() (relative/percentage change) — they answer different questions.

cards.prompt: Compute the day-over-day percentage change in ts's revenue. Fill in the blank.
cards.why: pct_change() expresses the change relative to the previous value (as a fraction), rather than diff()'s absolute difference.
cards.whenToUse: Growth-rate reporting, where a relative change matters more than the raw amount.
cards.commonMistake: Forgetting the first row is always NaN — there's no prior value to compare against.

cards.prompt: Compute a running total of ts's revenue from the start of the series. Fill in the blank.
cards.why: cumsum() accumulates every value from the beginning through the current row — never resets, unlike a rolling window.
cards.whenToUse: Total-to-date metrics, like cumulative revenue or a running balance.
cards.commonMistake: Expecting cumsum() to reset per group automatically — combine it with groupby() explicitly if you need per-group running totals.

cards.prompt: Track the highest revenue seen so far at each point in ts. Fill in the blank.
cards.why: cummax() carries forward the running maximum — once a new high is hit, it stays until an even higher value appears.
cards.whenToUse: A 'best value to date' metric, like an all-time-high tracker.
cards.commonMistake: Expecting the running value to ever decrease — a cumulative max can only stay flat or increase, never drop.

cards.prompt: Compute an exponentially weighted moving average of ts's revenue with a span of 3. Fill in the blank.
cards.why: Unlike rolling(), which weights every row in the window equally, ewm() weights recent rows more heavily — 'span' controls how quickly older rows fade out.
cards.whenToUse: Smoothing that should react faster to recent changes than a plain rolling average would.
cards.commonMistake: Expecting ewm() to produce NaNs like rolling() does at the start — by default it returns a value from the very first row, weighted only by what's been seen so far.

cards.prompt: Compute the range (max minus min) within every 3-day rolling window of ts's revenue.
cards.why: rolling().apply() runs a custom function against each window when no built-in aggregation (.mean(), .sum()...) covers what you need.
cards.whenToUse: A window statistic that isn't one of the built-in rolling aggregations.
cards.commonMistake: Reaching for rolling().apply() when a built-in exists — e.g. rolling(3).std() is both simpler and faster than a custom lambda replicating standard deviation.

cards.prompt: Instead of looking backward, get tomorrow's revenue alongside every row — shift the Series backward by 1. Fill in the blank.
cards.why: A negative shift argument looks forward instead of backward — shift(-1) pulls each row's value up from the next row.
cards.whenToUse: Comparing a row to what comes next, e.g. checking if tomorrow's value will be higher.
cards.commonMistake: Assuming shift() only looks backward — the sign of the argument controls the direction entirely.

cards.prompt: Which computes a running total using every prior row from the start, rather than a fixed-size window?
cards.why: expanding() always includes every row from the beginning through the current one — rolling() only looks at a fixed-size trailing window, and diff().cumsum() computes something else entirely (a running total of the changes, not of the values).
cards.whenToUse: A 'total to date' style metric where the window should keep growing, never staying a fixed size.
cards.commonMistake: Reaching for rolling() with a very large window size to approximate this — expanding() says exactly what's meant and needs no window-size guess.
